biography: Archdeacon of Aberdeen and a clerk in the service of Robert II; he travelled repeatedly to England and France for study (Oxford and Paris) and royal business. His Brus, completed c. 1375, earned him a royal pension, and he died on 13 March 1395.
literary_profile: Author of The Brus (c. 1375), a verse chronicle of the wars of independence celebrating Robert Bruce and James Douglas; other works attributed to him (including a Troy book) are lost.
stylistic_characteristics: Energetic octosyllabic couplets; vivid battle narrative and stirring speeches; the celebration of freedom ('A! Fredome is a noble thing!') within a providential frame.
intellectual_concerns: Scottish independence and national identity; the virtue of freedom against tyranny; chivalric loyalty.
historical_significance: The father of Scottish poetry and of Scottish national historical literature; the Brus is the first great work in Older Scots.
major_influences: the French romance and chanson de geste tradition
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his other works are lost, so the canon rests on the Brus alone.

biography: A blind poet or minstrel ('Blind Hary') who composed the Wallace c. 1477, reciting it before James IV for payment; royal treasury records note payments to him in the 1470s and 1490s. Almost nothing else is known of his life.
literary_profile: Author of The Wallace (c. 1477), an epic verse life of William Wallace in heroic couplets, drawing on the lost biography by John Blair and on oral tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: Robust, declamatory couplets; fierce anti-English sentiment and graphic battle scenes; the folk-heroic exaggeration of Wallace's deeds.
intellectual_concerns: Scottish freedom and the cult of Wallace; loyalty and betrayal; national memory.
historical_significance: The Wallace was for centuries the most popular book in Scotland after the Bible (Burns acknowledged its inspiration) and fixed the popular image of Wallace for posterity.
biographical_uncertainty: Nearly everything about him is conjectural; dates approximate.

biography: A university graduate ('Master') who served as schoolmaster of the grammar school of Dunfermline and as a notary public; his name appears in the records of Dunfermline Abbey in 1478. He died c. 1500. The finest of the fifteenth-century makars, he is grouped by Dunbar among the dead poets of the Lament for the Makaris.
literary_profile: Author of the Morall Fabillis of Esope (c. 1480s), the Testament of Cresseid (c. 1475–90), Orpheus and Eurydice, Robene and Makyne, and a body of shorter moral poems.
stylistic_characteristics: Chaucerian forms infused with northern speech; rueful, compassionate irony; the beast fable raised to satiric and philosophical art; mastery of the 'ballat royal' stanza.
intellectual_concerns: Justice, prudence, and the social order; the tragedy of Cresseid as a drama of sin, punishment, and late repentance; mortality and consolation.
historical_significance: Universally ranked with Dunbar as the greatest of the makars; his Testament of Cresseid is the most powerful continuation of Chaucer ever written, and his Fabillis the summit of the European fable tradition in the vernacular.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; almost nothing is known of his life beyond the Dunfermline records.

biography: A graduate of St Andrews (MA 1479) and a Franciscan novice in his youth, he served from c. 1500 as a clerk and poet at the court of James IV, for whom he wrote the celebratory poems of the marriage to Margaret Tudor (1503); he received a royal pension from 1500. He disappears from record after the battle of Flodden (1513), and died c. 1520.
literary_profile: Author of some eighty poems preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne and Maitland manuscripts: the Lament for the Makaris (c. 1505), The Goldyn Targe, The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo (c. 1500–07), the flying with Kennedy, the dream allegories, and the great occasional verse of the court.
stylistic_characteristics: The most technically virtuosic of the makars: aureate magnificence (The Goldyn Targe) alternating with scabrous colloquial satire (the Tretis); the refrain, the flying, the alliterative line, and the French formes fixes all mastered; a voice by turns celebratory, venomous, elegiac, and devout.
intellectual_concerns: The vanity of life and the power of death (Timor mortis conturbat me); the hypocrisies of court and clergy; the duties and pleasures of the royal court.
historical_significance: With Henryson, the greatest poet of medieval Scotland; the Lament for the Makaris is one of the supreme elegies in the language and gave the Scottish tradition its name.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; his clerical status and career details are conjectural.

biography: Captured at sea by the English in 1406 at the age of eleven, he spent eighteen years as a prisoner at the English court, where he received a full education in the company of Henry V's courtiers and poets. Released in 1424, he returned to rule Scotland with reforming vigour until his murder by conspirators at Perth on 21 February 1437.
literary_profile: Traditionally credited with The Kingis Quair (c. 1424), the dream vision in which the captive narrator sees his beloved and is consoled by the goddesses of love and fortune; the attribution rests on the poem's own claims and manuscript tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: Graceful Chaucerian rhyme royal with an autobiographical frame; the fusion of Boethian consolation with courtly love vision; precociously Renaissance delight in nature and architecture.
intellectual_concerns: Love, fortune, and providence; the education and duties of a prince; captivity and deliverance.
historical_significance: The Kingis Quair is the fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition and one of the great prison poems of European literature.
biographical_uncertainty: The attribution of the Quair to James I is traditional and widely accepted but not absolutely certain.

biography: A priest and secretary or chaplain to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for whom he composed the Buke of the Howlat (c. 1448); he later joined the exiled Douglases in England, was forfeited with them, and died c. 1483, perhaps in Orkney.
literary_profile: Author of the Buke of the Howlat (c. 1448), an alliterative beast-allegory in which the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the birds to the pope and emperor, a satire on pride, flattery, and the Douglas family's enemies.
stylistic_characteristics: The northern alliterative long line in intricate thirteen-line stanzas; the beast parliament as political allegory; a blend of heraldic pageantry and moral satire.
intellectual_concerns: Pride and humility; the flattery of courts; the honour of the Douglas family.
historical_significance: The Howlat is the last major alliterative poem of the Scottish tradition and a key document of Douglas politics and northern heraldry.
biographical_uncertainty: Little is known of him; dates approximate and career reconstructed from Douglas records.

biography: An Augustinian canon and prior of Lilleshall Abbey, Shropshire, active in the 1380s and 1390s; he compiled the Festial, a cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, with a companion instructional work for parish priests (Instructions for Parish Priests).
literary_profile: Author of the Festial (c. 1380s) and Instructions for Parish Priests, among the most widely copied English sermon collections of the later Middle Ages.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, lively English sermons built on exempla, miracles, and verse tags; the vivid storytelling of popular piety adapted for parish preaching.
intellectual_concerns: The instruction of the laity in the feasts, sacraments, and moral duties of the church year.
historical_significance: The Festial is the classic collection of the English late medieval sermon and a principal witness to orthodox vernacular preaching in the age of Lollardy.
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; details come almost entirely from his own prefaces.

biography: An Augustinian friar of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, and doctor of divinity (Cambridge), who composed his Legends of Holy Women between 1443 and 1447 at the request of East Anglian patrons, several of them women. He died c. 1464.
literary_profile: Author of the Legends of Holy Women (1443–47), a collection of thirteen verse saints' lives — including those of Margaret, Anne, Katherine, Cecilia, and Mary Magdalene — with a substantial autobiographical prologue; also a prose treatise on the Mappula Angliae (a translation of Higden).
stylistic_characteristics: Lydgatean verse with aureate diction; the female saint's life treated with tenderness and dramatic force; an unusually self-revealing authorial voice.
intellectual_concerns: The cult of female sanctity and its patronage by devout women; the legitimacy of vernacular hagiography.
historical_significance: The Legends are the principal fifteenth-century English monument of the female saints' lives and a major document of literary patronage by women.
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; his career before the 1440s is unknown.

biography: Born at Lynn on 21 April 1393, he studied at Cambridge, joined the Augustinian friars, and became prior of their house at Lynn; he travelled to Rome in 1450 and died on 12 August 1464. The most learned English writer of his generation, he composed in both Latin and English.
literary_profile: Author of the Life of St Katharine (c. 1445), the Life of St Norbert, the Abbreuiacion of Cronicles, the chronicle of England to 1417, the pilgrimage guide Ye Solace of Pilgrimes, and numerous Latin commentaries and lives.
stylistic_characteristics: Learned, well-ordered prose and Lydgatean verse; the devout scholar's care for accuracy and orthodoxy; the blending of chronicle and hagiography.
intellectual_concerns: The cult of St Katharine and the defence of learning; English history in the Lancastrian interest; orthodox devotion against Lollardy.
historical_significance: The leading East Anglian man of letters of the mid-fifteenth century; his Katharine is a classic of the learned saint's life.
biographical_uncertainty: Little uncertain: his own works and the Lynn records document his career closely.

biography: Of Welsh or Breton descent and educated probably at Oxford, he spent most of his career as a canon of St George's chapel, Oxford; in 1152 he was consecrated bishop of St Asaph in Wales, a see he may never have visited, and he died c. 1155. His Historia Regum Britanniae made him one of the most influential writers of the European Middle Ages.
literary_profile: Author of the Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136–38), the Prophetiae Merlini (c. 1135), and the Vita Merlini (c. 1150), which together created the Matter of Britain.
stylistic_characteristics: Elegant, deliberately classicizing Latin prose; the fabrication of a continuous British history from Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest; the vivid set-pieces of Arthur's reign and the prophecies of Merlin.
intellectual_concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the British (Welsh) past; the legitimation of Norman rule through Trojan descent; prophecy as political instrument.
historical_significance: The Historia created the Arthurian legend as a European literary possession and shaped British historiography for four centuries; without it there is no Brut, no Grail cycle, no Malory.
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; the sources of his 'British book' remain the central problem of Arthurian scholarship.

biography: A monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey, where he spent his whole career, becoming precentor and, late in life, refusing the abbacy; he died c. 1143. The greatest English historian since Bede, he gathered his materials from libraries across England and corresponded with the learned of his day.
literary_profile: Author of the Gesta Regum Anglorum (first version 1125, revised to c. 1135), the Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125), the Historia Novella (c. 1140–43), and saints' lives including those of Wulfstan, Dunstan, and Aldhelm.
stylistic_characteristics: Polished, allusive Latin modelled on classical historians; critical assessment of sources; a gift for anecdote and character; patriotic pride in English history tempered by Norman loyalties.
intellectual_concerns: The continuity of the English kingdom from the Anglo-Saxons to his own day; the moral exemplarity of history; the recovery of the English past after the Conquest.
historical_significance: The founder of critical English historiography after Bede; his Gesta Regum is the principal narrative source for Anglo-Norman history and the model for the century's chroniclers.
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; his Anglo-Saxon sources were largely lost in the Reformation.

biography: Son of a Norman clerk and an English mother, and archdeacon of Huntingdon from c. 1110, he was commissioned by Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, to write a history of England; he travelled with the court, visited Rome (1139), and continued revising his Historia Anglorum until his death c. 1157.
literary_profile: Author of the Historia Anglorum (first version 1129, continued to 1154), the most widely read English chronicle of the twelfth century, and of verse epigrams including the satirical De contemptu mundi.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, vivid narrative with a moralist's relish for battles, plagues, and the falls of great men; the ubi sunt meditation and the contemptus mundi theme; patriotic celebration of the English past.
intellectual_concerns: The providential shape of English history; the transience of earthly power; the continuity of the English people through conquest.
historical_significance: The Historia Anglorum is a principal source for the Norman and Angevin periods and the classic expression of twelfth-century historical moralism.
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; details of his career rest on his own book.

biography: Grandson of Nest, the Welsh princess, and of a Norman baron; educated at Paris, he became archdeacon of Brecon and courtier of Henry II, accompanying Prince John to Ireland in 1185 and preaching the crusade through Wales with Archbishop Baldwin in 1188. He twice sought the see of St Davids and was twice refused; retired to Lincoln, he died c. 1223, still writing.
literary_profile: Author of the Topographia Hibernica (1188), Expugnatio Hibernica (1189), Itinerarium Cambriae (1191), Descriptio Cambriae (1194), and the autobiographical De Rebus a Se Gestis, among much else.
stylistic_characteristics: Vivid, gossipy, self-promoting Latin; ethnography seasoned with marvel and prejudice; the love of a good story over strict accuracy; an unflagging attention to his own career.
intellectual_concerns: The Welsh church's independence; the conquest and description of Ireland; the character and customs of the Welsh and Irish peoples.
historical_significance: The Itinerarium and Descriptio are the classic medieval accounts of Wales, and the Expugnatio the principal narrative of the English conquest of Ireland; his works are foundational for both national historiographies.
major_influences: his uncle the bishop of St Davids
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; his own writings, though copious, are self-serving.

biography: A Herefordshire-born clerk of Welsh descent who studied at Paris and served Henry II as a royal justice and travelling ambassador; he attended the Lateran Council of 1179 and became a canon of St Paul's and archdeacon of Oxford. The archsatirist of the Angevin court, he died c. 1210.
literary_profile: Author of De Nugis Curialium (Courtiers' Trifles, c. 1181–92), a miscellany of satire, gossip, marvels, and history that preserves some of the earliest Arthurian and fairy material in Latin; the Goliardic poems once attributed to him are not his.
stylistic_characteristics: Biting, allusive, deliberately disordered satire of the court and the religious orders; the anecdote raised to moral fable; a proto-Renaissance pessimism about the world he served.
intellectual_concerns: The vices of courts and monasteries; the vanity of worldly service; the relations of the sexes; the marvels of Wales and the Celtic past.
historical_significance: De Nugis is the supreme literary monument of the twelfth-century courtier's disenchantment and a key source for the early Arthurian and Herla/fairy traditions.
biographical_uncertainty: Dates approximate; the De Nugis survives in a single manuscript and its text is unstable.

biography: Educated at Paris under the greatest masters of the twelfth-century schools — Abelard, William of Conches, Gilbert of Poitiers — he returned to England as secretary to Archbishop Theobald and then to Thomas Becket, whose exile he shared and whose murder he witnessed (1170). He became bishop of Chartres in 1176 and died there on 25 October 1180.
literary_profile: Author of the Policraticus (1159), the first great medieval treatise on political theory; the Metalogicon (1159), a defence of the trivium; the Historia Pontificalis; and a celebrated correspondence.
stylistic_characteristics: Classical learning worn lightly and worn for moral ends; the organic metaphor of the body politic; satiric portraits of courtiers; the first medieval theory of tyrannicide.
intellectual_concerns: The limits of royal power; the education of the prince and the clerk; the relation of church and state; the value of humane letters.
historical_significance: The Policraticus is the most important political treatise between Augustine and Aquinas and the fountainhead of medieval constitutionalism; its organic state theory shaped political thought for centuries.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his Paris studies is reconstructed from the Metalogicon.

biography: A monk of St Albans from 1217, he succeeded Roger Wendover as the abbey's chronicler in 1236 and made St Albans the foremost centre of English historical writing; friend and correspondent of Henry III, he travelled to Norway (1248) and died in 1259. He wrote, copied, and illuminated his own manuscripts with maps and drawings of exceptional skill.
literary_profile: Author of the Chronica Majora (begun c. 1240, continued to 1259), the greatest English chronicle of the thirteenth century; also the Historia Anglorum (abbreviation), the lives of the two Offas and of St Alban, and the Gesta Abbatum.
stylistic_characteristics: Vivid, opinionated, encyclopedic narrative; fierce criticism of the king, the papacy, and the friars; the integration of maps, itineraries, and marginal drawings into the historical record.
intellectual_concerns: The liberties of the English church and kingdom against papal and royal encroachment; the moral judgement of rulers; the recording of contemporary events from documents and eyewitnesses.
historical_significance: The Chronica Majora is the indispensable narrative source for the reign of Henry III and a landmark of medieval book art as well as of historiography.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; his surname may reflect continental training.

biography: Born on 24 January 1287, he became tutor to the future Edward III, and thereafter the king's trusted servant: keeper of the privy seal, chancellor (1334–35), and bishop of Durham from 1333. An insatiable collector, he assembled one of the greatest libraries in England, and his household probably produced the Philobiblon, completed shortly before his death on 14 April 1345.
literary_profile: Author (or patron-author) of the Philobiblon (1344), the celebrated Latin treatise on the love of books, their care, and their lending — the first bibliophilic classic in English literature.
stylistic_characteristics: Elegant, allusive Latin prose; the book personified as the companion of wisdom; practical rules for the custody of manuscripts enlivened by satire on careless clerks and students.
intellectual_concerns: The preservation and circulation of learning; the duties of clergy and princes to books; the reform of the universities.
historical_significance: The Philobiblon is the foundational text of English bibliophilia and a precious record of fourteenth-century book culture; de Bury's library fed Durham's later collections.
biographical_uncertainty: The precise authorship of the Philobiblon (de Bury or his chaplain Robert Holcot) is debated.

biography: Educated at Oxford and Paris, where he lectured on Aristotle, he joined the Franciscans c. 1257 and, frustrated by the neglect of experimental science, sought the patronage of Pope Clement IV, for whom he composed the Opus Maius, Opus Minus, and Opus Tertium in 1267–68. He was condemned by his order c. 1278 and imprisoned, and died c. 1292.
literary_profile: Author of the Opus Maius (1267), a programmatic encyclopedia of the sciences — mathematics, optics, experimental science, moral philosophy, and the reform of learning — together with works on grammar, astronomy, alchemy, and the calendar.
stylistic_characteristics: Urgent, polemical, encyclopedic prose; the advocacy of mathematics and experiment ('scientia experimentalis') as the foundation of knowledge; prophetic visions of technology (ships, cars, flying machines).
intellectual_concerns: The reform of the universities and of the church through science; the study of languages and texts; the practical power of knowledge.
historical_significance: The greatest scientific mind of the medieval West before the fourteenth-century natural philosophers; his experimental program made him the patron figure of early modern science in England (and the hero of Victorian legend).
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and the chronology of his Oxford years approximate; the circumstances of his condemnation are unclear.

biography: The subtlest of the scholastic philosophers: he entered the Franciscans c. 1280, studied and taught at Oxford and Paris, and lectured on the Sentences at Oxford c. 1300–02 and Paris 1302–05; transferred to Cologne in 1307, he died there on 8 November 1308. His thought defined one of the two great schools of late medieval theology.
literary_profile: Author of the Ordinatio (his revision of the Oxford Sentences lectures, c. 1300–08), the Quaestiones Quodlibetales, and treatises on metaphysics, logic, and natural theology, including his famous proof of God's existence.
stylistic_characteristics: Rigorous, compressed, terminologically innovative argument; the 'formal distinction' and the univocity of being; a dialectical subtlety that earned him the title Doctor Subtilis.
intellectual_concerns: The univocity of being and the nature of metaphysics; the freedom of God and of the will; the Immaculate Conception; individuation (haecceitas).
historical_significance: Founder of Scotism, which rivalled Thomism for centuries and shaped theology into the Reformation; among the most influential British philosophers of all time.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and early life approximate; the authenticity of parts of the corpus remains disputed.

literary_identity: philosopher; logician; political theorist; Franciscan friar
biography: A Franciscan who studied and taught at Oxford, where his teaching was denounced to the papal court at Avignon (1324); while awaiting judgement he became embroiled in the Franciscan poverty controversy, fled Avignon with Michael of Cesena in 1328, and spent the rest of his life under the protection of the emperor Louis of Bavaria at Munich, writing political works against the papacy until his death in 1347.
literary_profile: Author of the Summa Logicae (c. 1323), the Ordinationes on the Sentences, the Quodlibeta, and a series of political treatises on poverty and papal power.
stylistic_characteristics: The 'razor' of terminist logic: relentless elimination of superfluous entities and distinctions; a new theory of signs and mental language; clear, devastating polemic in the political works.
intellectual_concerns: The foundations of logic and knowledge; universals and nominalism; the limits of papal power; apostolic poverty.
historical_significance: The most consequential English philosopher of the Middle Ages: his nominalism reshaped European philosophy and theology (via Buridan, the via moderna, and Luther), and his political theory laid groundwork for conciliarism and modern notions of sovereignty.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his early works rests on internal evidence.

biography: A Benedictine monk of St Werburgh's abbey, Chester, where he spent his whole career, dying on 12 March 1364; his Polychronicon, a universal history and geography compiled from earlier writers, became the standard history of England, translated into English by John Trevisa in 1387 and printed by Caxton in 1482.
literary_profile: Author of the Polychronicon (completed c. 1327, continued to 1352), with its celebrated first book describing the geography of the world and of Britain, and of the Ars Componendi Sermones and other didactic works.
stylistic_characteristics: The industrious compiler's art: orderly encyclopedic arrangement, clear Latin, and a moralizing attention to the marvellous; the Polychronicon's world-description was a favourite of later chroniclers and cartographers.
intellectual_concerns: The unity of sacred and secular history; the description of the world and of Britain; the moral instruction of the clergy.
historical_significance: The Polychronicon dominated English historical writing for two centuries and, in Trevisa's translation, became one of the great monuments of fourteenth-century English prose.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his continuations of the Polychronicon are hard to separate from those of his successors.
